title: People you disagree with
hookLine: Bhai Kanhaiya's water for both sides
tomorrow: a rich man's feast or a carpenter's bread: where did Guru Nanak eat?

cards: Intramural soccer, Thursday, and the other team includes Cole, the junior from the bus stop, the one who flicked Arjan's patka. He goes up for a header, lands wrong, and stays down, holding his ankle. Simran is closest.
She's got a full water bottle in her hand. Behind her, a teammate mutters: let him limp. Part of Simran agrees.
She's already walking over, and still not sure why. Sikhs have an old story for exactly this moment, and they don't all read it the same way.

teach.h: WATER FOR THE WOUNDED, BOTH SIDES.
teach.b: Sikh tradition tells it like this. During the battles around Anandpur, a Sikh named Bhai Kanhaiya carried a leather water bag across the field, giving water to anyone wounded, Sikh soldiers and the soldiers fighting them.
Some Sikhs brought him to Guru Gobind Singh: he's reviving the enemy. The Guru asked him why.

teach.h: NO FRIEND, NO ENEMY, ONE LIGHT.
teach.b: Kanhaiya said he saw no friend and no enemy, only the Guru's face in every person. And tradition says the Guru blessed him, and handed him balm for their wounds as well.
The first reading: Kanhaiya is the whole teaching in one picture. Guru Nanak sings on Ang 13, in paraphrase, that the light is in everyone, and that light is the One. A thirsty man is a thirsty man.
The second reading speaks for the Sikhs who complained. They weren't cruel. They'd watched those same soldiers attack their families, and they knew the healed might come back to fight.
The Guru blessed Kanhaiya, and the Sikhs still defended Anandpur. Mercy to the wounded didn't mean the fighting had been nothing. Both readings keep something true.
Water for the hurt person is owed.

teach.h: THE OTHER VIEW: THE WRONG STILL HAPPENED.

teach.b: Simran kneels, hands Cole the bottle, and says: that was a bad landing.
Neither of them mentions the bus stop. Neither of them forgets it.

how: Sikhs tell the story of Bhai Kanhaiya when talking about seva for everyone, including people on the other side of a fight.

games.q: what does “people you disagree with” mean?
o: caring for someone hurt even when you still disagree
staying away from anyone whose views upset you
agreeing with others just to keep the peace at home

games.q: two readings, one story — tap the pairs.
p: water for the wounded on both sides
blessed him and gave him balm
a thirsty man is a thirsty man
mercy, and the wrong still happened

s: Guru Gobind Singh scolded Bhai Kanhaiya for helping the enemy
tradition says the Guru blessed him and handed him balm for their wounds as well.
helping someone who hurt others means saying it didn't matter
both readings keep it true: water for the hurt is owed, and the wrong still happened.
Guru Nanak sings that the light is in everyone, and that light is the One

games.q: your cousin says Bhai Kanhaiya was naive: the soldiers he helped went back to fight. what's the best case for Kanhaiya?
o: he saw the same light in every face; a thirsty man is still a thirsty man.
the Guru told him to weaken the enemy in secret by being kind to them.
the soldiers he helped had promised never to fight the Sikhs again.
games.why: Kanhaiya said he saw no friend and no enemy, only the Guru's face. the other reading is fair too: the Sikhs still defended Anandpur. mercy, without pretending.

practice: Close your eyes and bring to mind someone you strongly disagree with, not someone dangerous, just someone hard. Picture them tired, or thirsty, or hurt.
Without deciding anything about who was right, wish them one ordinary good thing, like a good night's sleep, and stay with that wish for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: People you disagree with. Bhai Kanhaiya's way: water for anyone who's hurt, without pretending the disagreement isn't real.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: jot, light. Ang 13: the light is in everyone, and that light is the One.

carryVoice: Hold onto it: water for both sides, the light in every face. A bad landing, a full bottle, day 1732.

sources.ref: The Bhai Kanhaiya tradition (water for the wounded at Anandpur), summarized
Ang 13, Dhanasari, Guru Nanak, in Sohila ('sabh meh jot jot hai soe'), paraphrased
